reader_summary.headline: Hello everyone and welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Raddai.
reader_summary.overview: Hello everyone and welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Raddai. I'm your host, Adipalmian and with me in the studio is my friend and colleague, Niklas Savos. In this episode we are delighted to have Phil Rosensvig on the show.

key_points.text: For nearly 30 years, Phil has been a professor at one of the world's leading centers for management research and education.
key_points.evidence_quote: For nearly 30 years, Phil has been a professor at one of the world's leading centers for management research and education, the IMD Business School in Los Angeles, Switzerland.

key_points.text: So Niklas, which book will we speak about?
key_points.evidence_quote: So Niklas, which book will we speak about?

key_points.text: Today we will speak about Phil's legendary book, The Halo Effect.
key_points.evidence_quote: Today we will speak about Phil's legendary book, The Halo Effect, which debunks a lot of the classic management literature such as Jim Collins built to last and good to great.

key_points.text: Phil explains how we tend to think that when a company performs well, the CEO is fantastic.
key_points.evidence_quote: Phil explains how we tend to think that when a company performs well, the CEO is fantastic, the company has operational excellence and the employees love to work there.

positions.commentary: The speaker notes Cisco was the most valued company before the bubble burst but states his story is not about Cisco itself.
The speaker mentions Apple was the most admired company for many years but questions if they are good at everything due to the halo effect.
The speaker acknowledges Nvidia did well with AI chips but expresses suspicion that their reputation carries over to other things unfairly.
The speaker bought Microsoft stock in 1991 and still holds it, stating he is pleased with the investment.
The speaker describes HP as a great company that was progressive and enlightened, though it no longer is.
The speaker notes that Andy Grove's book is wonderful and that Intel has suffered in recent years, but the basic lessons remain good.

thesis: This episode argues that a company's strong reputation in one area often unfairly extends to other areas where it may not be competent, a phenomenon known as the halo effect. The speaker illustrates this by questioning whether admired companies like Apple and Nvidia are truly good at everything, while noting that GE's past reputation may have masked underlying issues.
